title: Putting Back the Surroundings, and Blaming a Mutation

scenes.tts: Most cortical interneurons are born in another region, the ventral forebrain. So how could a cortical organoid get them?
scenes.visual: Title card: Putting Back the Surroundings, and Blaming a Mutation. A cortical organoid with an empty amber outline where interneurons should arrive.
scenes.narration: Most cortical interneurons are born in another region, the ventral forebrain. So how could a cortical organoid get them?

scenes.tts: Supply the region. In twenty seventeen, Sergiu Pashka's group at Stanford grew the two regions separately.
scenes.caption: Supply the region. In 2017, Sergiu Pașca's group at Stanford grew the two regions separately.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Birey, Andersen, Makinson, Pașca and colleagues, Stanford, 2017. A dorsal (cortical) spheroid and a ventral (subpallial) spheroid side by side.
scenes.narration: Supply the region. In 2017, Sergiu Pașca's group at Stanford grew the two regions separately.

scenes.tts: They labelled the ventral cells, then let one spheroid of each kind fuse.
scenes.visual: The ventral spheroid's cells turn gold. The two spheroids are pressed together and merge into one.
scenes.narration: They labelled the ventral cells, then let one spheroid of each kind fuse.

scenes.tts: Predict. Which way will the labelled cells move? And how?
scenes.visual: Question card over the fused pair: which way, and how?
scenes.narration: Predict. Which way will the labelled cells move? And how?

scenes.tts: They moved from the ventral partner into the cortical one, far more often than the reverse.
scenes.visual: A broad stream of gold cells crosses from the ventral side into the cortical side; only a trickle goes the other way.
scenes.narration: They moved from the ventral partner into the cortical one, far more often than the reverse.

scenes.tts: They moved in jumps. A leading process extends. A swelling forms ahead of the nucleus. Then the nucleus follows.
scenes.visual: Inset: one gold cell's jump in three steps, labelled process extends, swelling forms, nucleus follows.
scenes.narration: They moved in jumps. A leading process extends. A swelling forms ahead of the nucleus. Then the nucleus follows.

scenes.tts: Fetal interneurons move the same way. Once inside, the cells received excitatory synaptic input.
scenes.visual: Side by side, a fetal interneuron makes the same jump. In the cortical spheroid, synapses light up on a migrated gold cell.
scenes.narration: Fetal interneurons move the same way. Once inside, the cells received excitatory synaptic input.

scenes.tts: Then came cells from people with Timothy syndrome, caused by a mutation in a calcium channel gene.
scenes.visual: Label: Timothy syndrome, a gain-of-function mutation in CACNA1C, the gene for the L-type calcium channel Cav1.2.
scenes.narration: Then came cells from people with Timothy syndrome, caused by a mutation in a calcium channel gene.

scenes.tts: Patient interneurons made more jumps, but shorter ones. Overall, they moved less efficiently.
scenes.visual: Two tracks: control, fewer long jumps; patient, more short jumps covering less ground. Label: less efficient.
scenes.narration: Patient interneurons made more jumps, but shorter ones. Overall, they moved less efficiently.

scenes.tts: Fused to control cortex, patient interneurons still showed the defect. So it lay at least partly in the interneurons themselves. Blocking L-type calcium channels improved their migration.
scenes.visual: A gold patient ventral spheroid fused to a control cortical spheroid; the short-jump track appears again. Then a channel-blocker icon, and the patient track lengthens.
scenes.narration: Fused to control cortex, patient interneurons still showed the defect. So it lay at least partly in the interneurons themselves. Blocking L-type calcium channels improved their migration.

scenes.tts: Those two experiments, not the channel's location, point to a defect in the cells' own program. An assembloid can show it.
scenes.visual: Teal ticks beside the two experiments, the fused hybrid and the channel blocker. Label: evidence for a defect in the cells' own program.
scenes.narration: Those two experiments, not the channel's location, point to a defect in the cells' own program. An assembloid can show it.

scenes.tts: A host restores more. Human organoids were transplanted into newborn rat cortex. As the rats matured, the grafts gained a blood supply and responded to whisker deflection.
scenes.visual: A human organoid placed into a newborn rat's cortex. A card reads months later. In the older rat the graft is threaded with amber vessels and lights up when a whisker moves. Credit: Pașca's group, 2022.
scenes.narration: A host restores more. Human organoids were transplanted into newborn rat cortex. As the rats matured, the grafts gained a blood supply and responded to whisker deflection.

scenes.tts: In twenty thirteen, Lancaster and colleagues grew organoids from a person with microcephaly, a brain far smaller than normal. The patient carried mutations in a gene called C D K five R A P two. The patient's organoids had smaller progenitor zones. Is the mutation to blame?
scenes.visual: Credit card: Lancaster, Knoblich and colleagues, 2013. Label: CDK5RAP2. A patient organoid with small progenitor zones beside a control organoid.
scenes.narration: In 2013, Lancaster and colleagues grew organoids from a person with microcephaly, a brain far smaller than normal. The patient carried mutations in a gene called CDK5RAP2. The patient's organoids had smaller progenitor zones. Is the mutation to blame?
scenes.caption: In 2013, Lancaster and colleagues grew organoids from a person with microcephaly, a brain far smaller than normal. The patient carried mutations in a gene called CDK5RAP2. The patient's organoids had smaller progenitor zones. Is the mutation to blame?

scenes.tts: Predict. Name three other explanations, and a control that tests each.
scenes.visual: Question card: three other explanations, and a control that tests each.
scenes.narration: Predict. Name three other explanations, and a control that tests each.

scenes.tts: The rest of that person's genes. Several donors help, but only moving the gene itself really tests this.
scenes.visual: Card 1: genetic background. Control organoids from several people appear beside it; the card stays, stamped tested, not removed.
scenes.narration: The rest of that person's genes. Several donors help, but only moving the gene itself really tests this.

scenes.tts: A quirk of one cell line. Several clones from the patient test that.
scenes.visual: Card 2: a quirk of one line. Several patient clones appear beside it; the card is stamped tested.
scenes.narration: A quirk of one cell line. Several clones from the patient test that.

scenes.tts: A bad batch. Grow patient and control side by side, more than once.
scenes.visual: Card 3: a bad batch. Patient and control dishes side by side, repeated; the card is stamped tested.
scenes.narration: A bad batch. Grow patient and control side by side, more than once.

scenes.tts: These controls strengthen the comparison. Then move the gene itself. Put back into patient tissue, C D K five R A P two kept more cells as radial glia.
scenes.visual: CDK5RAP2 is delivered into patient tissue; more of the cells that received it keep radial glial shape.
scenes.narration: These controls strengthen the comparison. Then move the gene itself. Put back into patient tissue, CDK5RAP2 kept more cells as radial glia.
scenes.caption: These controls strengthen the comparison. Then move the gene itself. Put back into patient tissue, CDK5RAP2 kept more cells as radial glia.

scenes.tts: Reduced in control tissue by two different hairpin R N As, it let cells shift toward neurons.
scenes.caption: Reduced in control tissue by two different hairpin RNAs, it let cells shift toward neurons.
scenes.visual: Two different hairpin shapes, labelled CDK5RAP2 knockdown, enter control tissue; progenitors turn into neurons in both.
scenes.narration: Reduced in control tissue by two different hairpin RNAs, it let cells shift toward neurons.

scenes.tts: Why was the organoid a good bet? The protein works at the centrosome, inside the dividing progenitor. The rescue and knockdown, done in organoid tissue, made it a result.
scenes.visual: A dividing progenitor with its CDK5RAP2-bearing centrosome highlighted in teal, labelled the bet. Beside it, ticks for rescue and knockdown, labelled the result.
scenes.narration: Why was the organoid a good bet? The protein works at the centrosome, inside the dividing progenitor. The rescue and knockdown, done in organoid tissue, made it a result.

scenes.tts: If a gene acted through blood vessels or microglia, a normal-looking organoid would not clear it.
scenes.visual: An organoid looks normal; beside it, amber blood vessels and microglia are missing, with a question mark.
scenes.narration: If a gene acted through blood vessels or microglia, a normal-looking organoid would not clear it.

scenes.tts: Use the program to choose where to start. Then test the organoid, hardest where the surroundings matter, and measure every feature, because the dish adds stress of its own.
scenes.visual: Closing rule card, teal and amber, labelled a first guess: start with the program; test hardest where the surroundings matter; measure every feature.
scenes.narration: Use the program to choose where to start. Then test the organoid, hardest where the surroundings matter, and measure every feature, because the dish adds stress of its own.
